rationale: The book's case succeeds on the two things the task requires: it answers the strongest counter-reading, and its cited texts substantially carry its identification. Against the common 'oil = Holy Spirit' reading, the negative argument is scripturally sharp. First, the Torah itself separates 'oil for the light' from 'spices for anointing oil' (Ex 25:6; 27:20 vs Ex 30:22-33), which means most of the common interpretation's proof texts (1 Sam 16:13; Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38; 1 John 2:20) concern anointing/appointment oil, not lamp oil — they undercarry the popular claim. Second, the parable's own mechanics resist the Spirit reading: the oil must be bought (Matt 25:9), stored in advance, and cannot be transferred, whereas Scripture insists the Spirit is an unpurchasable gift (Acts 8:20), can be given instantaneously (Acts 10:44), and is not a zero-sum commodity (John 3:34). Third, the book handles the strongest counter-text, Zechariah 4, honestly: the angel's own decoding names the olive branches 'the two anointed ones' (4:14) and never equates the oil with the Spirit; 4:6 addresses the power behind Zerubbabel's work. On the positive side, the identification is carried by a coherent chain: Prov 6:23 fixes lamp = commandment; Matt 5:16 fixes light = visible good works; Prov 21:20 gives the exact triad of wise/fool/oil-stored-vs-squandered; Prov 23:23 ('buy the truth... wisdom, instruction') matches the parable's otherwise-odd command to 'buy' oil; and Ezek 36:27 preserves the Spirit as cause while distinguishing His produced obedience — so the reading does not banish the Spirit but locates Him correctly as source rather than symbol. Notably, this conclusion converges with the substantial patristic and historical reading (oil as works/obedience), so it is not an eccentric outlier but a scripturally tighter version of an established alternative. Remaining objections (below) are real but not decisive against the comparative question asked.
decisive_sources: Exodus 25:6 with Exodus 27:20 and 30:22-33 (lamp oil and anointing oil are separate provisions, disqualifying anointing-based Spirit proof texts)
Matthew 25:9 with Acts 8:20 (the parable's oil must be bought; the Spirit explicitly cannot be)
Proverbs 21:20 (wise store oil, the fool spends it — the parable's exact inventory)
Proverbs 23:23 (the command to 'buy' truth, wisdom, and instruction, matching the parable's verb)
Proverbs 6:23 with Matthew 5:16 (lamp = commandment, light = visible good works, leaving oil as what converts profession into lived obedience)
Zechariah 4:6-14 (the angel identifies the branches as 'the two anointed ones,' never equating oil with the Spirit)
Ezekiel 36:27 (the Spirit as cause of obedience, distinguishing the Spirit from His stored fruit)
unresolved_objections: Psalm 141:5 ('oil upon the head') and Proverbs 27:9 (ointment/perfume) are not lamp-oil contexts; the book bars the Spirit reading from importing anointing verses yet imports head-oil and perfume verses for its own definition, a methodological asymmetry
Zechariah 4's golden oil flowing to the lamps can still plausibly figure the Spirit's supply given 4:6's placement within the lampstand vision; the book's reading is defensible but not compelled
Mainstream critical scholarship's caution that the oil is a narrative detail of readiness, not a fixed allegorical referent, applies with equal force to the book's own detailed decoding

The composite definition ('Spirit-taught truth AND correction AND proven obedience') is broader than any single cited text establishes; each element is supported but their fusion into one referent is the book's synthesis
The book's ranked table of common interpretations is anecdotal (an AI-generated estimate) rather than evidence
